finding.headline: Plan for your money to last to age 98.
About 16% of your pay goes to tax now, and retirement tax looks very low.
details: Today you pay about $14,124 in total tax on $86,000 of pay, which is an effective rate of 16%.
Your savings are all in cash and taxable accounts, so the plan draws on those first, then pre-tax accounts, then Roth accounts.
In retirement, the plan estimates about $104 a year in tax on withdrawals of about $33,504 a year. This is a rough guide, not tax advice.

finding.headline: At 61, you can contribute more to your 401(k) for 2027, and Medicare starts at 65, four years away.
details: Ages 60 to 63 may contribute a higher catch-up amount of $11,750 to a 401(k) for 2027, instead of $8,500.

Your plan says you retire at 63, but Medicare generally starts when you turn 65, which is 2 years after you retire. Sign up during your 7-month Initial Enrollment Period, which runs from 3 months before you turn 65 to 3 months after, to avoid a late penalty that grows the longer you wait.

finding.headline: This household has no children, pets, or college costs to plan for.
details: Family costs total $0, so no yearly family spending ends at a set age. Your basic needs after retiring come to about $42,000 a year, or $3,500 a month.

Health coverage before Medicare at age 65 is about $10,000 a year, so plan for that gap from age 63 until Medicare starts. Long-term nursing home care, if needed, is about $129,575 a year for 3 years, so it is worth planning for.
Your debts total $10,800, with yearly payments of $3,600. Paying the 27.58% credit card first would cut the most interest.

finding.headline: Your spending goal of $72,000 a year did not last in any of 100 market scenarios.
details: The plan kept was a simple plan with 15 points less in stocks, since no similar household's plan did better. In 0 of 100 scenarios the household paid its basics all the way to age 98, and the money ran out in all 100.
The most you can spend and still be safe in 90 of 100 scenarios is $33,100 a year, about $2,758 a month. That is 46% of your $72,000 goal, so the gap is $38,900 a year.

Savings are $23,600 today and you are not adding to them, so the cushion is small. Markets are uncertain, and these results are not promises. Lowering spending or raising savings before retirement would matter most.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.
Your spending now is about $2,924 a year more than your take-home pay, so until you retire the plan takes that from your savings each year. If that is wrong, change your spending now or your pay.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.

Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $38,600 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 67 for you and 69 for your partner, which pays about $41,600 a year.
A partner with little pay of their own gets half of the other's benefit at 67, less if started sooner.
After the first death (at the shorter life expectancy), Social Security falls to the larger of your two benefits, about $21,800 a year, and spending falls to 75% of what the two of you spend.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 98. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that one of you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
